items.passage:
From Wooden Frame to Safety Bicycle: How the Bicycle Changed

The bicycle may look simple, but it took many years of experiments to reach its modern form. The first widely recognized ancestor appeared in Germany in 1817. Karl Drais, a German inventor, built a wooden machine with two wheels that a rider pushed along with his feet. Because it had no pedals, it was often called the "running machine." It was expensive and hard to balance on, but it showed that a person could travel quickly on two wheels.

In the 1860s, a French craftsman named Pierre Michaux and his workers added pedals to the front wheel. This made the machine faster, but it also made the front wheel much larger, since each turn of the pedals moved the bicycle only a short distance. The result was the high-wheeled "penny-farthing," which was exciting to ride but dangerous. Falling from such a great height often caused serious injuries, so many people were reluctant to ride it.

The solution came in the 1880s with the "safety bicycle." Its two wheels were nearly the same size, and a chain connected the pedals to the back wheel. Riders sat lower and could control the machine more easily. The design was further improved in 1888 when John Boyd Dunlop, a Scottish veterinarian, developed a pneumatic tire filled with air. Air-filled tires absorbed bumps and made riding far more comfortable.

Today, the bicycle is used for transportation, sport, and leisure all over the world. Its basic design has remained almost unchanged for more than a century, which shows how well the safety bicycle solved the problems of its earlier versions.

A Surprising First Day

When I first heard that a new transfer student would be joining our class, I was not particularly excited. Most of us had been friends for years, and I thought that a new person might disrupt our comfortable routine. I expected him to be quiet and perhaps a bit shy, so I didn't think much about how to welcome him.

On Monday morning, the teacher introduced a boy named Leo. He was much taller than I expected and had a bright, energetic smile. Instead of sitting at the back of the room as I had imagined, he walked straight to a seat near me and said, "Hi, I'm Leo. I hope we can be friends!" His confidence was quite surprising, and I felt a little nervous about my own response.

During the lunch break, I noticed Leo sitting alone in the cafeteria, looking at a map of the school. I remembered that I had been lost on my first day, too, so I decided to approach him. When I asked if he was looking for something, he looked up and laughed, saying he was trying to find the library. We ended up talking about our favorite hobbies, and I discovered that we both loved playing basketball.

By the end of the day, my initial worries had completely disappeared. I realized that I had been wrong to assume he would be a disruption. Instead, Leo's arrival brought a fresh energy to our classroom, and I was glad that I had taken the first step to talk to him.

items.passage:
The Changing Role of Robots in Modern Healthcare

In recent years, the use of robots in hospitals has moved from science fiction to a practical reality. While many people may imagine robots replacing human doctors, the current trend is actually toward "collaborative robotics." These machines are designed to work alongside healthcare professionals to improve the efficiency and safety of medical services. By taking over repetitive or physically demanding tasks, robots allow nurses and doctors to spend more time focusing on direct patient care.

One of the primary roles of robots in hospitals is logistics and delivery. For instance, autonomous mobile robots are now frequently used to transport medicine, laboratory samples, and meals to different departments. These machines can navigate complex hallways and elevators without human intervention. This reduces the workload on hospital staff, who previously had to spend a significant portion of their shifts moving supplies between rooms. In a busy urban hospital, this change can lead to faster response times for patients in need of urgent medication.

Furthermore, robots are playing an increasingly important role in surgery and rehabilitation. Surgical robots, controlled by skilled surgeons, enable high-precision procedures that are difficult to perform with human hands alone. These tools can make smaller incisions, resulting in less pain and quicker recovery times for patients. In rehabilitation centers, wearable robotic suits help patients with mobility issues practice walking again. These technologies do not replace the human touch; instead, they provide advanced tools that enhance the quality of care provided by medical experts.

The Letter from Berlin

Last summer, I finally received the long-awaited letter from my pen pal, Klaus. We had been writing to each other for over two years via email, but he always insisted on sending traditional postcards or letters by mail when we met during our annual video calls. This time, his letter arrived with a stamp featuring a bear, which I immediately recognized as a souvenir from the Berlin Zoo.

Klaus explained that he had traveled to a small village in Bavaria last month while visiting his grandparents. He was supposed to stay for only three days, but the weather turned unexpectedly cold and rainy. Because of this sudden change, he decided to extend his stay by two more days to wait out the storm with his family. During those extra days, he explored an old castle nearby and even tried local traditional bread making under his grandmother's supervision.

However, the most important part of his letter was not about the trip itself, but about a small misunderstanding that occurred on the third day. Klaus had promised to send a postcard every week from different places in Germany. On this particular day, he forgot to mail one because he got distracted by helping his neighbor fix a bicycle wheel. He felt terrible about breaking his promise and wrote this letter as an apology. I could feel his sincere regret through the words on the page.

To make up for the delay, Klaus included three postcards from his favorite spots in Bavaria attached to the envelope. He also mentioned that he is planning to visit my hometown next year if our schedules align. The news made me very happy, even though I missed having his weekly updates. Reading his story about the rainy days and the bicycle wheel repair gave me a new appreciation for how things can go wrong in unexpected ways. Klaus ended his letter by asking me to send him some Japanese snacks when he returns to Berlin, promising to try them before sending another reply.

The Letter from Berlin

Last summer, I finally received the long-awaited letter from my pen pal, Klaus. We had been writing to each other for over two years via email, but he always insisted on sending traditional postcards or letters by mail when we met during our annual video calls. This time, his letter arrived with a stamp featuring a bear, which I immediately recognized as a souvenir from the Berlin Zoo.

Klaus explained that he had traveled to a small village in Bavaria last month while visiting his grandparents. He was supposed to stay for only three days, but the weather turned unexpectedly cold and rainy. Because of this sudden change, he decided to extend his stay by two more days to wait out the storm with his family. During those extra days, he explored an old castle nearby and even tried local traditional bread making under his grandmother's supervision.

However, the most important part of his letter was not about the trip itself, but about a small misunderstanding that occurred on the third day. Klaus had promised to send a postcard every week from different places in Germany. On this particular day, he forgot to mail one because he got distracted by helping his neighbor fix a bicycle wheel. He felt terrible about breaking his promise and wrote this letter as an apology. I could feel his sincere regret through the words on the page.

To make up for the delay, Klaus included three postcards from his favorite spots in Bavaria attached to the envelope. He also mentioned that he is planning to visit my hometown next year if our schedules align. The news made me very happy, even though I missed having his weekly updates. Reading his story about the rainy days and the bicycle wheel repair gave me a new appreciation for how things can go wrong in unexpected ways. Klaus ended his letter by asking me to send him some Japanese snacks when he returns to Berlin, promising to try them before sending another reply.

My First Day at the Riverside Cafe

When I saw the "Help Wanted" sign in the window of the Riverside Cafe, I felt both excited and nervous. I was sixteen, and it was my first time applying for a real job. I had never made coffee for anyone except my parents, so I was not sure I could do it. Still, I walked in and asked for an application form.

The manager, Mrs. Hayashi, was a calm woman with silver hair. She read my form quickly and smiled. "You don't need experience," she said. "You need patience and a willingness to learn." Her words made me feel a little better. A week later, she called me and offered me a job on Saturday mornings.

My first shift was on a rainy Saturday in March. I arrived fifteen minutes early, wearing an apron that was far too big for me. Mrs. Hayashi showed me the espresso machine, the cash register, and the list of drinks. I tried to memorize everything, but my head was spinning. Within an hour, I had already spilled milk on the counter and mixed up two orders.

At first, I wanted to hide in the storeroom. However, a regular customer, an elderly man who always ordered black coffee, noticed my trembling hands. He winked at me and said, "Everyone starts somewhere, young man." His kindness gave me the courage to keep going.

By noon, I was working more smoothly. I remembered the orders, cleaned the tables, and even laughed when a little girl asked me to draw a cat in the foam of her hot chocolate. When my shift ended, Mrs. Hayashi handed me my first paycheck and said, "You did well today."

Walking home that afternoon, I realized that I was no longer afraid of making mistakes. I was proud of myself, and I couldn't wait for my next Saturday at the cafe.

items.passage:
Lost in Translation

When I arrived at the airport in Melbourne, I was nervous. It was my first time living abroad, and I had only three months to study at a high school there as an exchange student. My host family, the Parkers, met me at the arrival gate with a big sign that said "Welcome, Yuki!" I felt a little better right away.

The first week was full of surprises. At breakfast, Mrs. Parker asked me if I wanted a "cuppa." I smiled and nodded, thinking it was some kind of special tea. When she handed me a mug of plain tea with milk, I realized that "cuppa" simply meant "cup of tea." I laughed, and so did she.

Things became harder at school. On my second day, my homeroom teacher asked me to introduce myself to the class. I stood up, spoke slowly, and said I liked "football." Everyone looked confused. Then a boy named Liam said, "Oh, you mean soccer!" I felt my face turn red. In Australia, "football" usually means Australian rules football, so I had made a small but embarrassing mistake.

The biggest surprise came at lunch. I had prepared a sandwich, but I saw that my classmates were sharing food from one big box in the middle of the table. Nobody seemed to mind that they were eating each other's snacks. In Japan, we usually keep our own food separate, so I hesitated. Then Emma offered me a biscuit, and I took it. It tasted wonderful, and I began to understand that sharing was a way of showing friendship.

Looking back, I think those small misunderstandings helped me. Each time I got something wrong, I learned something new about my host country and about myself. By the end of the three months, I was no longer afraid of making mistakes. I was simply excited to see what would happen next.

The Changing Role of Robots in Modern Healthcare

In recent years, the use of robots in hospitals has moved from science fiction to a practical reality. While many people may imagine robots replacing human doctors, the current trend is actually toward "collaborative robotics." These machines are designed to work alongside healthcare professionals to improve the efficiency and safety of medical services. By taking over repetitive or physically demanding tasks, robots allow nurses and doctors to spend more time focusing on direct patient care.

One of the primary roles of robots in hospitals is logistics and delivery. For instance, autonomous mobile robots are now frequently used to transport medicine, laboratory samples, and meals to different departments. These machines can navigate complex hallways and elevators without human intervention. This reduces the workload on hospital staff, who previously had to spend a significant portion of their shifts moving supplies between rooms. In a busy urban hospital, this change can lead to faster response times for patients in need of urgent medication.

Furthermore, robots are playing an increasingly important role in surgery and rehabilitation. Surgical robots, controlled by skilled surgeons, enable high-precision procedures that are difficult to perform with human hands alone. When I became the captain of the high school soccer team last year, I felt a heavy sense of responsibility. During the middle of the season, our team faced a difficult period. We lost three matches in a row, and the atmosphere in the locker room became very tense. Some players started to argue with each other, and many seemed to lose their confidence. I felt frustrated and worried, but I knew I had to do something to change the situation.

Instead of focusing only on our mistakes, I decided to hold a small meeting after practice one evening. I sat down with everyone and shared my own feelings of disappointment. I admitted that I was also scared of losing. This honesty seemed to surprise my teammates, and soon, they began to open up about their own struggles. We talked about our fears and listened to each other’s opinions with respect.

From that day on, the mood changed completely. We started to support one another more actively during practice. Although we did not win every game, we finished the season with a sense of unity that I had never felt before. I learned that true leadership is not about being the best player, but about building a bridge between people.

The Day the Trains Stopped

I still remember the morning of February 8th, when I woke up to a silence that felt strange. Outside my window, the whole street was covered in thick white snow. I checked my phone and saw a message from my train company: "Due to heavy snow, all lines are suspended until further notice." I groaned. I had an important history test that day, and I had planned to arrive at school early to review my notes.

I hurried to the station anyway, pulling my scarf up over my nose. When I arrived, the platform was crowded with people staring at a large board that showed nothing but red letters. Nobody knew when the trains would start again. An old man beside me sighed and said, "I have been waiting here for two hours already."

I felt frustrated and worried. Then I noticed a girl about my age sitting on a bench, sharing her hot chocolate with a little boy who was crying because he was cold. Her kindness changed my mood. I decided to stop worrying about the test and do something useful. I walked to a nearby convenience store and bought some hot tea for the people who were waiting in the cold.

By noon, the station staff announced that a few trains would run slowly. A cheer rose from the crowd. I boarded a train with the girl and the boy, and we talked about how strange the day had been. When I finally reached school, the test had already begun. My teacher looked at my wet shoes and gave me a sympathetic smile, and she let me take the test in the library.

Looking back, I realized that the day had not gone the way I had planned, but I had learned something more important than any test score. Sometimes a small act of kindness can make a cold day feel warm.

The Hike That Almost Went Wrong

Last summer, my older brother Ken and I decided to climb Mount Hotaka, a peak in the Japanese Alps. We had planned the trip for months. We packed our bags the night before, checked the weather forecast, and saw that it would be sunny in the morning with only a small chance of clouds in the afternoon. I was excited, and I thought we would be back at the bottom by lunchtime.

We started early. The trail was steep, but the views were wonderful. By nine o'clock, we had reached a wide ridge, and I could see the valley below us covered in a soft white mist. Ken took a photo and said, "This is why we came."

Around ten, the sky changed quickly. Dark clouds rolled over the peaks, and a cold wind began to blow. Within twenty minutes, the trail was hidden in fog, and rain started to fall. I pulled out my phone to check the forecast, but there was no signal. I felt my stomach drop. I had trusted the forecast too much and had not brought a backup plan.

Ken stayed calm. He looked at the map, found a small shelter marked about one kilometer away, and told me to stay close behind him. We walked slowly, shouting to each other through the rain so we would not get separated. My hands were numb, and my boots were soaked, but I kept my eyes on Ken's red jacket.

After nearly an hour, we reached the shelter. We sat inside, shivering, and ate the snacks we had saved. Slowly, the rain stopped, and a thin patch of blue appeared above us. We waited another hour before starting down, but by then we were both tired and quiet.

Looking back, I realized how lucky we were. The trip did not go as planned, but Ken's calm decision made all the difference. I learned that a good mountain trip depends not only on the weather, but also on preparation and on trusting the people beside you.

Stepping onto the Stage

When I entered Kawaguchi High School in April, I had no plans to join any club. I had spent most of my middle school years playing basketball, but a knee injury during the spring tournament had forced me to stop. I told myself that I would simply go home after class and focus on my studies.

That plan changed on a rainy afternoon in May. While walking past the small auditorium, I heard a loud burst of laughter coming from inside. I peeked through the half-open door and saw a group of students reading lines from a script. One of them, a tall girl with a clipboard, noticed me and waved me in. Her name was Aya Mori, and she was the director of the drama club.

"We need one more actor for our autumn play," she said. "Do you want to try?"

I almost said no. Acting had never been part of my life, and I was sure I would freeze the moment I stood in front of people. Still, something in her warm smile made me hesitate. Before I could change my mind, I found myself reading a short line from the script.

My voice shook badly, and my face felt hot. The others, however, did not laugh at me. Instead, they gave me encouraging nods and asked me to try again. By the end of the hour, I had read the same line a dozen times, and it had become a little easier each time.

I joined the club that week. Over the following months, I spent countless evenings practicing lines, painting scenery, and learning how to breathe before speaking. Although I still felt nervous, I began to enjoy the feeling of standing under the bright lights.

On the night of the performance in October, I looked out at the full audience and felt my heart pound. Then I remembered the rainy afternoon and the friendly faces that had welcomed me. I took a deep breath and began to speak. For the first time in a long while, I felt truly alive.

items.answer: remove
items.hint: 空所の後ろにある「your shoes」が何をする対象かに注目してください。部屋に入る前にどうするかを考えます。
items.explanation:
訳: 部屋に入る前に、靴を脱いでください。

「部屋に入る前に靴を○○してください」という文なので、靴を身につけた状態から外す意味の語が入ります。「remove」は「取り除く」という意味で、ここでは「靴を脱ぐ」の意味になります。recommend（勧める）、submit（提出する）、inform（知らせる）は、靴を対象にしても意味が通りません。

答え: remove（取り除く）

items.passage:
The Science Behind Volcanoes

Have you ever wondered how massive mountains, known as volcanoes, are created? While they may seem like simple hills, volcanoes are actually complex openings in the Earth's surface. They are formed when molten rock, called magma, from deep inside the Earth rises to the surface. When this magma reaches the ground, it erupts and cools, eventually building up the structure of a volcano over many years.

There are several ways these geological formations can occur. One common method happens at "subduction zones." This is where two tectonic plates—the large pieces of the Earth's crust—collide. As one plate is pushed down under another into the hot mantle, it melts. This melted rock, now called magma, becomes less dense than the surrounding rock and rises toward the surface. This process is responsible for many of the famous volcanic chains found along the edges of oceans.

Another way volcanoes form is at "divergent boundaries." This occurs when two tectonic plates pull away from each other. As the plates move apart, they create a gap that allows magma to rise from below to fill the space. This often happens on the ocean floor, creating long chains of underwater volcanoes. In some cases, these underwater eruptions can eventually grow large enough to rise above the sea level and become new islands.

Understanding how volcanoes form is essential for scientists. By studying the movement of tectonic plates and the behavior of magma, researchers can better understand the Earth's internal processes and prepare for potential eruptions.

options.text: It is developed by the melting of rocks in the hot mantle.
options.mistake: 一部だけ合っている

options.text: It is formed by the collision of two tectonic plates.

options.text: It is created by the cooling of magma on the Earth's surface.

items.answer: It is created by the cooling of magma on the Earth's surface.
items.hint: 第1段落の最後の一文を確認しましょう。
items.explanation:
本文では、マグマが地表に到達して噴出し、冷えることで、長い年月をかけて火山の構造が作られると述べられています。したがって、マグマが地表で冷えることによって火山の構造が作られるとする「マグマが地表で冷えることによって火山の構造が作られる」という選択肢が正解です。選択肢「プレートの衝突によって形成される」および「マントル中の岩石が溶けることによって発達する」は、火山の形成に関わるプロセスの一部ではありますが、火山の「構造」が作られる直接的な仕組みとしては不十分です。選択肢「地球の地殻の大きな断片の動きによって形作られる」は、プレートの動きが火山形成の要因の一つであることは示されていますが、構造がどのように作られるかという問いに対する直接的な答えにはなっていません。

本文の根拠: “When this magma reaches the ground, it erupts and cools, eventually building up the structure of a volcano over many years.”

items.passage:
A Lesson from the Podium

Last spring, I decided to participate in the school English speech contest. I had always been a shy person, and the idea of speaking in front of a large audience terrified me. However, I wanted to challenge myself and overcome my fear of public speaking.

I spent several weeks preparing my speech, which was about the importance of small acts of kindness in our community. I wrote the text many times and practiced reading it aloud in my room. Even though I knew my topic well, I still felt extremely nervous as the day of the contest approached.

When my name was finally called, my heart was racing. I walked up to the podium, and for a moment, my mind went completely blank. I looked out at the audience and saw dozens of faces waiting for me to speak. I felt a sudden urge to run off the stage, but then I remembered my practice. I took a deep breath, looked at the front row, and began to speak.

As I continued, my voice became steadier. I focused on the message I wanted to share rather than my own nervousness. When I finished, there was a moment of silence, followed by a warm round of applause. I did not win the first prize, but that was not what mattered most to me. The real victory was the feeling of accomplishment I had when I stepped down from the stage. I realized that courage is not the absence of fear, but the ability to move forward despite it.

To find a way to improve their public speaking skills.

options.text: To share their knowledge about community activities.

items.answer: To overcome the fear of speaking in front of others.
items.hint: 第1段落の後半部分を確認してください。
items.explanation:
「恐怖を克服したい」という動機が書かれているため、多くの人の前で話すことへの恐怖を乗り越えることが目的である「overcome the fear of speaking in front of others」が正解となります。
「win the first prize」は、第4段落で「1位になれなかった」と述べられているため、目的ではありません。
「improve their public speaking skills」については、挑戦したいという意図はありますが、スキル向上そのものが目的であるとは書かれていません。
「share their knowledge about community activities」は、スピーチの内容（親切な行為の重要性）についての記述であり、コンテストに参加した理由ではありません。

本文の根拠: “However, I wanted to challenge myself and overcome my fear of public speaking.”
